name: Lead acetate hair dye

lead: Lead acetate hair dyes were gradual hair darkeners, mostly sold to men, that covered gray by building up a darker tone over repeated combings or applications rather than changing hair color in one sitting. The result was a subtle, natural-looking shade that appealed to people who wanted younger-looking hair without an obvious dye job.

Regulators have since withdrawn the approval. The US FDA permitted lead acetate in scalp hair dye at up to 0.6 percent in 1980, then repealed that approval, concluding there was no longer a reasonable certainty of no harm; manufacturers moved to bismuth citrate.

paras: Historically users applied the product to dry hair repeatedly over days or weeks until the desired shade was reached, which let them control the depth of color. Products carried a required label warning. Today the same gradual-darkening approach is sold with lead-free colorants such as bismuth citrate, and consumers are advised by the FDA to check ingredient lists.

Lead is a neurotoxic metal and the FDA stated that no level of exposure is considered safe. The agency cited exposure from hands, scalp and surfaces, and children's contact with treated people or products. Health Canada banned lead acetate in cosmetics from the end of 2006, and the EU also prohibits it.

web.title: FDA repeal of lead acetate approval

chain: Lead compound reacts with hair keratin to deepen color
Gray covered with a gradual, natural-looking shade
angle.text: Progressive dyes covered gray hair, letting people restore a darker, more youthful-looking tone in small steps. Lead-free versions using bismuth citrate now serve the same goal.

lead: Lead acetate hair dye refers to the progressive or gradual hair colorants that used lead(II) acetate to darken gray hair over repeated use. The best-known example was Grecian Formula, a men's product, which the manufacturer reportedly kept using lead acetate in until 2018 before moving to bismuth citrate [1].

Users liked the controllable, gradual darkening, which avoided the abrupt look of a one-step dye. In 1980 the FDA listed lead acetate as a permitted color additive for scalp hair at up to 0.6 percent lead, requiring the label 'Contains lead acetate' [2].

The FDA repealed that listing in a rule that became effective on January 6, 2022, after a 2017 petition, saying that new information meant there was no longer reasonable certainty of no harm [3]. Canada banned the compound in cosmetics from the end of 2006 [1].
infobox: Banned in cosmetics from end of 2006

paras: Progressive dyes darken hair a little more with each use. Lead acetate was the active colorant in many of these products in low concentration, and Grecian Formula is the standard example among men's products [1]. The compound is also called sugar of lead because of its sweet taste, and it was historically used to sweeten wine, a practice linked to poisonings [1].

On October 31, 1980 the FDA listed lead acetate in 21 CFR 73.2396 for coloring scalp hair, with a cap of 0.6 percent lead, a warning label, and a ban on use on eyebrows, eyelashes and body hair [2]. After a 2017 petition the FDA issued a final rule in October 2018, which was stayed by objections; on October 7, 2021 it lifted the stay and set an effective date of January 6, 2022, with enforcement discretion for 12 months to let manufacturers reformulate [3].

The FDA's reasoning was that no level of lead exposure is considered safe, that the original exposure study had deficiencies, and that blood lead levels have fallen since 1980, so exposure from dyes is no longer insignificant [3]. It said some manufacturers had already switched to bismuth citrate [3]. Health Canada banned lead acetate in cosmetics effective at the end of 2006, and the EU also bans it [1].

Lead acetate is classed as a reproductive toxicant and neurotoxin, and regulators have described it as a probable human carcinogen [1]. The FDA's advice to consumers was to check ingredient lists for lead acetate and consider bismuth citrate alternatives [3].
Gradual gray cover is discussed alongside other grooming options for graying hair, such as permanent dye, semi-permanent color and toners. Lead-free gradual products now fill that niche.
No studies found on the cosmetic effect of lead acetate dyes. Broader toxicology research on lead exposure exists, and the FDA's decision drew on it [3].
